definition: Logistic Regression is a classification model that maps a linear score into a probability using the logistic function. It is widely used when the goal is to predict class membership, estimate odds, and produce a model that remains interpretable enough for business and technical review.
intuition: Model class probability directly, then threshold it for classification when needed.
mathematical_foundation:
$$
p(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta^T x)
$$

$$
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `p(y = 1 | x)` | Probability of class 1 |
| `\sigma` | Sigmoid function |
| `\beta` | Coefficients |
| `x` | Features |
advantages: Fast to train and effective as a classification baseline.
Supports regularization and scales well to high-dimensional features.
assumptions: Observations are independent unless the model explicitly accounts for dependence.
Perfect separation is absent or handled with an appropriate remedy.
The predictors have a linear relationship with the log-odds of the outcome.
limitations: Assumes a linear relationship between features and log-odds unless transformed or extended.
Can be affected by multicollinearity, separation, and severe class imbalance.
